rv.q: Few plays tackle subjects as complicated and consequential as race, gender and solidarity with both comedy and nuance more deftly than Dominique Morisseau’s Confederates.

The masterful strokes of playwright Dominque Morisseau, the visionary leadership of director Raymond O. Caldwell, and a brilliant tour de force cast make Confederates a crowning achievement at the Fountain Theatre.
Morisseau brings the two stories together without pretending that 164 years have erased the differences between them.

What comes across instead is a reductive melodrama, with mugging from the performers in place of a skilled delineation of their characters’ truths — as essential in farce as it is in kitchen sink drama.
Confederates features a fantastic cast and memorable performances.
Morisseau, the Tony Award-nominated playwright and MacArthur fellow, has constructed a remarkably inventive theatrical experience.
CONFEDERATES manages to inject humor and laughter into this very serious subject.

cn.t: Morisseau's dual-timeline drama about Black women 150 years apart earns mostly strong reviews for its powerful performances and thought-provoking themes, with one dissenting voice finding the parallel structure uneven.
